grammar_notes.text: The suffix 'mau' can be added to a noun stem to indicate 'place of'. For example, if 'Woccon' means a place name, then 'Woccan-mau' would mean 'place of Woccon'.

cultural_notes.text: The Woccon/Waccamaw people have been referred to by various names throughout history, including Guacaya (1521), Wococon (1606), and Wattomas (1714).
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: Names we have been called: Guacaya (Francisco Gordillo, 1521) Wococon (Virginiae item et Floridae Americae Provinciarum, nova descriptio.1606) Wattomas (Barnwell (1714), 1908: 31)

cultural_notes.text: The Woccon Indians primarily lived between Neuse River and one of its affluents, near present-day Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: The Woccon primarily lived between Neuse River and one of its affluents, near present-day Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina.

cultural_notes.text: The first mention of the Woccon appears to be by Lawson writing about 1701, who recorded 150 words of their language.

cultural_notes.text: 1683 Proprietors heard that settlers were making war on the Indians around Winyah Bay in order to obtain slaves. Although a 1703 law placed a duty of 20 shillings on each Indian slave exported.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: (Ind. Rep. Quarterly 1973, Vol. 7, No. 1)

cultural_notes.text: 1695- Cape Fear are constantly attacked by natives allied with SC (Charleston) so they become “Tribute Indians” and start saving shipwreck victims. They save 52 passengers from a New England ship.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: (MIlling 1969:20)

cultural_notes.text: 1699, September 23rd- Richard Traunter describes: “between us and the Sea A Nation of Indians called the Wacawn’s, being Caniballs, and Maneaters..
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: (Dahlberg)

cultural_notes.text: 1701 John Lawson records 120 fighting men, and two towns “Yupwareremau and Tooptatmeer” plus 500 inhabitants. Records 150 words of the language and identifies them as “Siouan stock.” Also says that a group have broken away from the main settlement and relocated southward.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: (New Voyage to Carolina)

cultural_notes.text: 1711-1713 Tuscarora War- we are asked to join the war effort by Barnwell (against the Tuscarora). Part of Capt. Bull’s Co. in Barnwell’s Army.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: (Barnwell 1908:31)

cultural_notes.text: 2 Woccon are arrested in VA and charged with leaving NC without permission. Woccon name disappears around the same time Waccamaw name appears.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 2 Woccon are arrested in VA and charged with leaving NC without permission. Woccon name disappears around the same time

cultural_notes.text: In 1712, James Moore JR. asks the Waccamaw and Cape Fears (known to be with the Woccon often) to join him against the Tuscarora.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1712- Waccamaw name is mentioned – James Moore JR. asks them and Cape Fears (known to be with the Woccon often) to join him against the Tuscarora.

cultural_notes.text: In 1715, during the Yamassee War, the Waccamaw joined the Yamassee and Cheraw in attacking South Carolina.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: -we join Yamassee and Cheraw -April 15, 1715 attack, along with a large number of other native nations, SC

cultural_notes.text: In 1715, the Waccamaw were attacked by Maurice Moore, defeated, and many were taken captive/enslaved.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: -Attacked by Maurice Moore in 1715, defeated, and many were taken captive/enslaved.

cultural_notes.text: The Waccamaw people lived between the Black and Sampit Rivers at Winyah Bay with 100 fighting men.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: living between Black and Sampit Rivers at Winyah Bay with 100 fighting men.

cultural_notes.text: In 1716, William Watis (Waties) Sr. was appointed as a special agent for trade at Winyaw.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1716 Charleston appointed special agent William Watis (Waties) Sr. as factor at Winyaw

cultural_notes.text: In 1718, the Waccamaw people had reportedly moved to the Black River.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: Reported by trader Meredith Hughes that they have moved to the Black River

cultural_notes.text: The Waccamaw town of several hundred people operated independently, having their own headman and fields. They cooperated with the Catawba nation.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: Waccamaw town of several hundred people operated independently- had own headman and fields Cooperated with Catawba nation

cultural_notes.text: Due to raids and enslavement by Seneca, Cherokee, and other groups, some Woccon had confederated with the Catawba.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: Some had confederated with the Catawba due to raids and enslavement by Seneca, Cherokee, and other groups

cultural_notes.text: In 1723, some Waccamaw sought refuge with the Winyaw and Pedee.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1723 some seek refuge with Winyaw -some with the Pedee

cultural_notes.text: A Catawba leader visited Charleston in 1727 to explain crimes committed by Waccamaws and Cheraws living amongst them. The Waccamaw village was a half mile from that of the Catawba leaders.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1727 Sept. “a Catawba leader and eight others visited Charleston to explain crimes committed by Waccamaws and Cheraws living amongst them

cultural_notes.text: Mooney (1894: 77) believes that the Waccamaw were finally incorporated with the Catawba, a view echoed by Hodge (1910: 887) and mentioned by Swanton (1952:101). It is possible they allied themselves with the Catawba or were absorbed by English settlements.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: Mooney (1894: 77) believes that the Waccamaw were finally incorporated with the Catawba, a view echoed by Hodge (1910: 887)

cultural_notes.text: The Waccamaw people are reported in the Low Country in 1728/1733.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1728/1733 they are reported in Low Country

cultural_notes.text: In 1749, a war broke out between the Waccommassus (Waccamaw) and South Carolina.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1749- War broke out between Waccommassus (Waccamaw, Waccamaw-Siouan website) and SC

cultural_notes.text: The Waccamaw people are last referred to as 'Settlement Indians' in 1755.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1755- being called “Settlement Indians”- last reference to the name “Waccamaw”

cultural_notes.text: In 1810, John Dimery purchases 300 acres in 'Dog Bluff'.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: 1810- John Dimery purchases 300 acres “Dog Bluff”

cultural_notes.text: The Woccon language closely resembled Catawba, and was considered one of two Catawban languages, which are part of the Siouan language family.
